docs.title: Language V4
docs.text:
So far our languages do not allow for anything like repetition. In an expression-based language (ours fall into this category), repetition is typically accomplished by recursion, and recursion depends on the ability to apply function recursively. So we need the ability to define and to call functions.

As a starting example, consider the following V4 program.

let
  f = proc(x) +(x, 3)
in
  .f(5)

Using V4's specification, this program evaluates to 8.

docs.title: A quick tour
docs.text: The declaration in the let expression defines a function using the proc keyword and assigns it a name (i.e., f). The let body applies the function using the dot character (.) with a single parameter (i.e., 5).

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Think of a function as a "black box" that, when given zero or more input parameters, returns a single result value. The number of parameters that a function accepts is called its arity.

To define a function means to describe how it behaves. To apply a function means to give the function the proper number of parameters and to receive its result. Formal parameters refer to the list of parameters appearing in a function definition. Actual parameters refer to the list of parameters appearing in a function application.

Using mathematical notation, we can define a function \(f\) by

\[ f(x) = x + 3 \]

and we can apply the function \(f\) by

\[ f(5) \]

The result of this particular application is \(8\).

docs.title: ProcVal
docs.text: In Language V4, functions are treated as values just like integers. In particular, we create a ProcVal class that extends the Val class. This implies that a ProcVal object can occur anywhere a Val object is expected.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
It is possible to define and to apply a function in one expression, such as

.proc(x) +(x, 3) (5)

The evaluation of both this expression and the program defined at the beginning of this chapter return the same value, namely the integer 8.

Notice, too, that proc(x) +(x, 3) also returns a value, but the value is a function, not an integer. (One’s intent when defining a function is eventually to apply it, although this is not a requirement.)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Below are several V4 programs using functions.

The following program

let
  f = proc(x, y) +(x, y)
in
  .f(3, 8)

evaluates to 11.

The second program

let
  f = proc(z, y) +(10, y)
in
  .f(3, 8)

returns 18.

Finally, this program

let
  x = 10
in
  let
    x = 7
    f = proc(y) +(x, y)
  in
    .f(8)

also returns 18.

In this third example, name x in the proc definition refers to the enclosing x (which is bound to 10), not to the inner name x (which is bound to 7). Remember the rules for evaluating the declarations in let expression!

Now consider the next three examples, all of which evaluate to 5:

let
  app = proc(f, x) .f(x)
  add2 = proc(y) add1(add1(y))
in
  .app(add2, 3)

let
  app = proc(f,x) .f(x)
in
  .app(proc(y) add1(add1(y)), 3)

.proc(f, x) .f(x) (proc(y) add1(add1(y)), 3)

In the first of these three examples, observe that we can pass a function (in this case add2) as a parameter to another function. This app function takes two parameters and returns the result of applying the first actual parameter to the second. Of course, the first parameter had better be bound to a function for this to work. (If it is not, an attempt to apply it throws an exception.)

In the second example, we have eliminated the identifier add2 and instead simply replaced add2 in the application .app(add2, 3) with the nameless function proc(y) add1(add1(y)) that used to be called add2.

In the third example, we have even eliminated the name app.

Finally consider the following example, which evaluates to 120:

let
  fact = proc(f, x)
    if x
    then *(x, .f(f, sub1(x)))
    else 1
in
  .fact(fact, 5)

This example, quite a bit more subtle than the previous ones, shows how you can achieve recursion — factorial, in this case — using our simple language (which does not yet support direct recursion!).

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
We are now prepared to add syntax and semantics to support functions. First we add grammar rules for function definition and application, and display their corresponding abstract syntax classes:

<Exp:ProcExp>    ::= <Proc>
def __init__(self, proc)
<Proc>           ::= PROC LPAREN <Formals> RPAREN <Exp>
def __init__(self, formals, exp)
<Formals>        **= <SYMBOL> +COMMA
def __init__(self, symbolList)
<Exp:AppExp>     ::= DOT <Exp> LPAREN <Rands> RPAREN
def __init__(self, exp, rands)

Obviously, appropriate definitions of PROC and DOT tokens must accompany these rules.

docs.title: ProcVal
docs.text:
Before we can go any further, we need to tackle the definition of a ProcVal, which is what we should get when we evaluate a ProcExp expression.

A ProcVal object must capture the formal parameters as an instance of the Formals class, and it must remember its function body as an instance of Exp. But what environment should we use to evaluate the function body when the function is applied? To conform to our notion of static scope rules, we want to evaluate the function body using the environment in which the function is defined. So any variables in the function body which are not among the formal parameters – in other words, the variables that occur free in the function body – are bound to their values in the environment in which the function is defined.

In programming languages terminology, the term closure refers to an entity that captures all of the ingredients necessary to apply a function. In Language V4 ProcVal objects are closures.

The attributes of the ProcVal class appear here:

class ProcVal(Val):

    def __init__(self, formals, body, env):
        self.formals = formals
        self.body = body
        self.env = env

Recall that we can do two things with a function: define it and apply it. We will discuss function definition shortly, but first we give the semantics of function application.

docs.title: Function application
docs.text:
The method eval in the AppExp class defines the semantics of function application.

AppExp
%%%
def eval(self, env):
    v = self.exp.eval(env)
    args = self.rands.evalRands(env)
    return v.apply(args, env)

Here are a description of these steps:

  1. Evaluate exp in the current environment; this evaluation must return a ProcVal object (a closure) with attributes consisting of the list o formals parameter, the function body, and the captured environment.
  2. Evaluate rands (the actual parameter expressions) in the current environment to get a list of Vals (the parameters). [Note: we did exactly the same thing when evaluating the rands of a PrimappExp.]
  3. Evaluate the body of the function with the current environment and actual arguments computed in the previous step.

The only thing we have left is to implement the behavior of the apply method in the Val class. Since we want apply only to be meaningful for a ProcVal object, we define a default behavior in the (abstract) Val class to throw an exception for anything but a ProcVal:

class Val:

    # Some Vals can be applied to a list of arguments (e.g. a ProcVal).
    # Like the evaluation of an expression, the application of a Val takes
    # place in the context of an environment, which arrives as the second
    # parameter. An applied Val may use or ignore that environment as its
    # own semantics require.
    def apply(self, args, env):
        raise LanguageError(f"Cannot apply {self}")

For a ProcVal, here is the implementation of apply:

class ProcVal(Val):
    def apply(self, args, env):
        if len(self.formals.symbolList) != len(args):
            raise LanguageError("formals/args number mismatch")
        bindings = Bindings(self.formals.symbolList, args)
        nenv = self.env.extendEnv(bindings)
        return self.body.eval(nenv)

These steps are as follows:

  1. Check that the number of actual parameters matches the number of formal parameters. If there is mismatch, throw an exception.
  2. Create bindings of the function’s list of formal parameters (formals) to the list of actual parameters passed as an argument (args).
  3. Use these bindings to extend the environment (env) captured by the function.
  4. Evaluate the body of the function in the (extended) environment (nenv).

docs.title: Function definition
docs.text:
Let us now examine the detailed semantics of a ProcExp, which is used to define a function.

As noted earlier, a ProcVal closure is constructed with instance attributes consisting of the list of formal parameters (a Formals object), the function body (an Exp object), and the environment in which the function is defined (an Env object).

The makeClosure method in the Proc class creates a ProcVal object given an environment:

Proc
%%%
def makeClosure(self, env):
    return ProcVal(self.formals, self.exp, env)
%%%

The semantics of the eval method in the ProcExp class is now trivial:

ProcExp
%%%
def eval(self, env):
    return self.proc.makeClosure(env)
%%%

docs.title: Language V5
docs.text:
We normally prefer to use direct recursion instead of relying on the contrived tricks described in the previous chapter. Specifically, we would like to write

let
  fact = proc(x) if zero?(x) then 1 else *(x, .fact(sub1(x)))
in
  .fact(5)

Unfortunately this program does not work as intended. Recall that in a let expression the expressions on the right-hand side of the declarations are all evaluated in the enclosing environment. Only after all the right-hand side expressions have been evaluated do we bind each of the left-hand side identifiers to the corresponding left-hand side results.

The above function's body refers to the identifier fact which is free in the definition. Indeed the identifier fact does not appear in the function's formal parameter nor does it appear in the enclosing environment which is empty. Thus an attempt to apply the function fails because of an unbound identifier.

To solve this problem, we create a new let-like expression that supports direct recursion. Called letrec, it allows us to define functions supporting direct recursion. The following is what we want:

letrec
  fact = proc(x) if zero?(x) then 1 else *(x, .fact(sub1(x)))
in
  .fact(5)

Evaluation of this program with V5 produces 120.

docs.title: A quick tour
docs.text: The syntax of a letrec expression is the same as its let counterpart. The difference lies in its semantics. Without going into details yet, the declarations are evaluated in such a way as to allow them to refer to each other. This evaluation strategy allows functions to call themselves recursively. Specifically, in the example above, the identifier fact in the right-hand side is bound to the same identifier in the left-hand side.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
We require a new token (LETREC) as well as a new grammar rule:

<Exp:LetrecExp>  ::= LETREC <LetDecls> IN <Exp>

This rule depends on two non-terminal symbols (LetDecls and Exp) which we have already defined in the context of the definition for let expressions.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
The right-hand side of the expressions appearing in the declaration are evaluated in the order in which they appear, using an environment where all of the previous bindings in the letrec are accessible. In addition, if the right-hand side expression is a function, it captures the entire environment created by all of the bindings in the letrec expression. This evaluation strategy means that functions defined in a letrec expression can refer to each other. In particular, they can call themselves recursively.

This is unlike a normal let, in which the right-hand side expressions are all evaluated in the enclosing environment, and the created bindings are only accessible in the body. Consequently, the right-hand side expressions of a let can be evaluated in any order, which is sometimes called parallel evaluation. The only difference between the semantics of the let and letrec expression is in the way in which we build the environment capturing the bindings issued from the declarations.

docs.title: Order matters
docs.text:
Because right-hand side expressions are evaluated in the same environment they update, the order in which declarations appear matters.

The program

letrec
  x = 3
  y = x
in
  y

evaluates to 3.

The downside to letrec expressions is that declarations cannot be evaluated in parallel. So, ideally, letrec should only be used when you need to define a recursive function.

docs.title: Declarations
docs.text:
To implement the recursive behavior of a letrec expression, we define a new method called addLetrecBindings in the LetDecls class.

LetDecls
%%%
def addLetrecBindings(self, env):
    env = env.extendEnv(Bindings())
    for sym, e in zip(self.symbolList, self.expList):
        val = e.eval(env)
        env.add(Binding(sym.lexeme, val))
    return env

This new method is passed the environment in which the letrec expression appears and returns a new environment. To do so, the method performs the following steps:

  1. Immediately extend the current environment with an empty set of bindings.

  2. In order,

  3. Evaluate each right-hand side expression in this new environment.

  4. Update the new environment with a new binding tying left-hand side identifier to the result of its corresponding right-hand side expression.

  5. Once all the declarations have been processed return the new environment.

Recall that the LetDecls initializer checks for duplicate left-hand side identifiers during parsing. Since the grammar rule for letrec reuses LetDecls, a letrec expression implicitly also makes this check.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Consider the following program:

letrec
  x = 5
  f = proc(t) *(t, x)
in
  .f(42)

The processing of its declaration proceeds as follows:

  1. Create a new environment by extending the enclosing environment with an empty list of bindings.
Env (new)bindingsEnvbindingsBindings
  1. In the order in which the left-hand side identifiers appear, create a binding of the left-hand side identifier (x and then f) to the value of its corresponding right-hand side expression (5 and then proc(t) *(t, x)) — where each right-hand side expression is evaluated in the extended environment — and add this binding to the extended environment.
ProcValformals : tbody : *(t, x)envBindingsx : 5fEnv (new)bindingsEnvbindings
  1. Once all of the bindings have been added to the extended environment, return the extended environment.

docs.title: Body
docs.text:
We can now evaluate a LetrecExp object in exactly the same way as a LetExp object:

LetrecExp
%%%
def eval(self, env):
    env = self.letDecls.addLetrecBindings(env)
    return self.exp.eval(env)

The key idea is to evaluate the right-hand side expressions of a letrec in an environment that (self-referentially) includes all of the declared bindings. Specifically:

  1. Extends the current environment with all the declarations.

  2. Evaluate the body in the extended environment.

docs.title: Mutual recursion
docs.text:
The letrec construct allows us to define mutually recursive functions — two or more functions that call each other recursively. Here’s a classic example:

letrec
  even? = proc(x) if zero?(x) then 1 else .odd?(sub1(x))
  odd? = proc(x) if zero?(x) then 0 else .even?(sub1(x))
in
  .even?(11)

This program evaluates to 0 (i.e., false).

Notice that we have used the character ? in the variable names for the functions to suggest that they should be considered predicates that return true (i.e., 1) or false (i.e., 0). We added this lexical feature to Languages V5 and beyond.

docs.title: Exercise 1
docs.text: Can you define the odd?/even? mutually recursive functions in Language V4, that is, without letrec?

docs.title: Going beyond
docs.text: The Scheme programming language introduced the letrec construct to enable the definition of mutually recursive functions.
